Bangladesh confirms deal to buy Chinese J-10 fighter jets: report. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has confirmed a deal to purchase China’s 4.5-generation J-10CE fighter jets, citing the aircraft’s reported combat performance against French-made Rafale jets during the brief Pakistan-India conflict in May, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported on Friday.

The Chengdu J-10C is a single-engine, multirole combat aircraft manufactured in China. Boasting a top speed of Mach 1.8, it can be fitted with a variety of air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions. It played a key role on the first night of hostilities, shooting down six jets belonging to the Indian Air Force.

The Information and Broadcasting Adviser to the Prime Minister of Bangladesh Zahedur Rahman said earlier this week that a draft proposal to buy the jets had been submitted to the country’s finance ministry and Armed Forces Division for final approval, SCMP reported citing the Bangladeshi Press Information Department (PID).

According to the Bangladesh PID, the draft proposal also includes the purchase of Chinese attack helicopters, VIP transport helicopters and drones.

“Subject to necessary budgetary allocation in the current fiscal year, this procurement will be executed immediately; otherwise, it will roll over into the next budget cycle,” it added.

SCMP reports that Rahman said Bangladesh “paid attention” to the war last year, when Pakistan used J-10 fighters and PL-15 long-range air-to-air missiles to shoot down Indian Rafales.

In January this year, Pakistan and Bangladesh’s air chiefs held detailed discussions on the “potential procurement” of the locally-produced JF-17 Thunder aircraft, according to Inter-Services Public Relations.

It added that Bangladesh Air Force Air Chief Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan called on Pakistan Air Force Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Babar Sidhu in Islamabad, where “The meeting focused on strengthening operational cooperation and institutional synergy, with emphasis on training, capacity building, and collaboration in aerospace advancements.”

A day later, Dhaka’s air chief discussed avenues for enhancing defence cooperation with Pakistan in separate meetings with Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff (COAS) Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Naveed Ashraf.

A year ago, Pakistan was engaged in a military conflict with India, dealing the boastful neighbour an internationally recognised “clear setback”.

The conflict with India, starting from the April 22 Pahalgam attack to the end of Operation Bunyanum Marsoos, with a ceasefire ending a military escalation between the two countries on May 10, has been called “Marka-i-Haq” (Battle of Truth) by the state.

But from the night of May 6 to May 10, the drums of war were echoing loudly across South Asia as the nuclear-armed arch-rivals exchanged missiles, raising global alarm over the risk of unpredictable escalation.

item.title: Extreme heat is climate injustice. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent finding that 22 million Bangladeshi children are now exposed to intensified heat should alarm every policy-maker in the country.
Extreme heat is no longer an abstract climate concern but a direct, daily threat to our children’s health, development, and future.
As one of the world’s most heat‑vulnerable nations, the fact that our children are paying the price for a crisis they did nothing to create should anger us deeply.
Heat affects children differently and more severely, increasing the risk of dehydration, respiratory distress, malnutrition, and long‑term developmental harm. It disrupts schooling, reduces outdoor play, and places enormous stress on families who must navigate rising temperatures without adequate cooling, shade, or healthcare access.
Protecting children from heat thus requires year‑round planning: Better heat‑resilient school infrastructure, shaded community spaces, early‑warning systems, and public health campaigns that help families recognize and respond to heat stress. Our urban planning must also recognize the importance of tree cover and ventilation.
With that said, while Bangladesh must do all it can to combat the effects of climate-change induced heat, it should not be shouldering this burden alone.
It bears repeating that wealthy nations have contributed to the climate crisis, yet it is countries like Bangladesh that bear the brunt of the consequences.
Protecting vulnerable children thereby requires climate finance that is predictable, adequate, and accessible. Grants - not loans - must support adaptation measures and technology transfers must be real, not rhetorical. Global climate negotiations must also stop sidelining the needs of heat‑exposed children in the Global South, treating them as if their concerns are secondary.
Bangladesh is doing what it can, but the scale of the crisis demands international responsibility. No child should suffer because the world’s richest countries failed to act time and time again.

item.title: Safety in the Rohingya camps must be ensured. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The killing of a five‑year‑old child in the Rohingya camps is a devastating reminder of how precarious life has become for those who sought refuge in Bangladesh.
The camps in Cox’s Bazar were meant to offer temporary safety to a population fleeing genocide and persecution. Instead, they have increasingly become sites of danger -- from landslides and fires to criminal violence and structural failures.
A child’s death under such circumstances therefore can no longer be simply dismissed as an accident but rather be seen as evidence of a system under severe strain.
Overcrowding, fragile terrain, and shrinking international aid have created conditions where even basic safety cannot be guaranteed. This was never supposed to be the situation in these camps.
Children, who make up a large share of the camp population, are the most vulnerable. When a retaining wall collapses or violence erupts, they are the ones who suffer first.
Bangladesh has shown extraordinary generosity by hosting more than a million Rohingya refugees -- this is an irrefutable fact. However, generosity alone does not ensure protection.
Camp safety must be treated as a core humanitarian priority, and Bangladesh cannot and must not be expected to shoulder this responsibility alone.
The need for stronger policing and community engagement is undeniable to prevent violence and protect the most vulnerable, yet this strengthening will not be possible under present circumstances.
International responsibility therefore is critical to ensuring that the situation doesn’t take a turn for the worse. Funding cuts have already reduced food rations, education services, and infrastructure maintenance.
A camp system starved of resources cannot keep people safe. Donor fatigue is not an excuse when children’s lives are at stake.
Safety in the Rohingya camps must be ensured -- with the seriousness every human life deserves.

item.title: The evolution of nationalism and the 'Bangladesh first' doctrine. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh emerged in 1971 through an emancipatory nationalism rooted in Bengali language, culture, democratic representation, and resistance to economic exploitation. Bengali nationalism supplied the moral energy of liberation.
Sovereignty, however, transformed the central political question. The issue was no longer only how Bengalis could achieve self-determination, but how the new republic could include every citizen, including communities that did not identify ethnically as Bengali.
This problem appeared during constitution-making when the citizenry was defined as Bengali. Manabendra Narayan Larma’s historic objection in the Constituent Assembly challenged the assimilation of peoples possessing their own languages, customs, and ancestral histories. His intervention exposed the distinction between cultural identity and constitutional citizenship.
The republic has since continued to negotiate the relationship between Bangalee cultural identity and Bangladeshi legal identity. In theoretical terms, this is the tension between an ethnocultural nation and a civic nation.
It was within this setting that Ziaur Rahman articulated Bangladeshi nationalism. Its principal innovation was to relocate national identity from exclusive ethnocultural markers to territorial sovereignty, citizenship, and common political destiny.
Citizens were united not by identical lineage or language, but by membership in an independent republic. The formulation emphasized territorial integrity, multiparty democracy, national production, rural development, cultural distinctiveness, and an independent foreign policy.
It sought to distinguish the sovereign identity of Bangladesh from the wider cultural geography of the Bengali-speaking world and to create an umbrella under which different ethnic and religious communities could coexist.
Begum Khaleda Zia inherited this tradition under different conditions. Her leadership against autocratic rule and the 1991 restoration of parliamentary government demonstrated that Bangladeshi nationalism could operate through electoral legitimacy.
It became associated with parliamentary politics, economic liberalization, export-led growth, and female education. Nevertheless, a winner-takes-all culture of boycotts, distrust, and executive control persisted. Tarique Rahman’s politics and the 31-Point State Reform Outline emerged as a response to this institutional crisis.
“Bangladesh first” may be understood as both a nationalist commitment and a doctrine of governance. Its central claim is that Bangladesh’s welfare, dignity, sovereignty, and decision-making autonomy must guide domestic policy and foreign relations.
This is not necessarily isolationism or autarky. It resembles strategic autonomy: International engagement remains indispensable, but partnerships must be assessed according to reciprocity, sustainability, and national interest.
In this sense, sovereignty is not withdrawal from the world; it is the capacity to engage the world without surrendering independent judgment.
The doctrine’s most important normative possibility lies in civic nationalism. Political membership should arise from equal citizenship, constitutional loyalty, and participation in common institutions -- not religious affiliation, ethnicity, or inherited status.
Accordingly, the language of merely “protecting minorities” should give way to the republican obligation to enforce universal rights. Minorities must not depend on majority benevolence. Their security, worship, dignity and political participation are enforceable constitutional entitlements.
Hannah Arendt’s famous phrase, “the right to have rights,” captures the point: Meaningful citizenship requires institutions that make rights real.
Formal equality, however, is insufficient where poverty prevents citizens from accessing food, healthcare, housing, and education. TH Marshall’s theory of social citizenship explains why civil and political rights must be accompanied by social rights.
From this perspective, the proposed Family Card and Health Card can be interpreted not as charity but as instruments of substantive citizenship.
They seek to protect low-income households, reduce food insecurity, expand primary healthcare, and strengthen maternal and child services.
Their legitimacy will depend on universal rules, transparent eligibility, and independent oversight. If distributed through partisan networks, welfare becomes clientelism; if administered through law, it can reinforce civic solidarity.
Cultural pluralism is equally necessary. Bengali language, literature, and the Liberation War remain foundational, but national culture also includes Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Garo, Santal, Manipuri, and other histories.
Unity creates a shared constitutional future; coercive uniformity produces alienation. A pluralist “Bangladesh first” must protect minority languages, include diverse histories in education, prosecute communal violence, and treat all religious and indigenous festivals as elements of the national inheritance.
The doctrine also advances a form of decentralized developmental nationalism. Political sovereignty remains fragile when economic life depends excessively on external finance, imported technology, a narrow export base, and extreme administrative centralization.
Economic sovereignty does not mean protectionist retreat; it means developing domestic capabilities so that global integration occurs from a position of resilience. Agricultural modernization, industrial diversification, technical education, and local production are therefore connected to national autonomy.
Decentralization is crucial. The principle of subsidiarity holds that decisions should be taken at the lowest effective level. Predictable fiscal transfers, elected local institutions, and participatory budgeting could enable communities to address local needs, reduce pressure on Dhaka and deepen participation beyond national elections.
Human-capital development is another pillar. Technical and vocational education in information technology, renewable energy, logistics, and healthcare can move Bangladesh beyond informal work and low-wage manufacturing.
Overseas employment should shift toward certified professional mobility, while diplomatic missions provide legal and emergency support. Citizen-centred nationalism must protect Bangladeshis wherever they work.
The doctrine returns to the Liberation War’s promises of equality, dignity, democracy, and social justice. Its ethic of “service over conflict” seeks to transform politics from a struggle for spoils into public responsibility and civic virtue.
Yet, party-based service must remain voluntary and non-partisan, never replacing the state or controlling public benefits. Internal accountability and zero tolerance for corruption and violence are indispensable.
The 31-Point Outline translates these values into institutional design. Prime-ministerial term limits seek to prevent personalized executive dominance. A bicameral legislature could widen deliberation by incorporating regional representation and specialized knowledge. Reform of Article 70 could allow members of Parliament greater independence on ordinary legislation while preserving stability on budgets and confidence votes.
Judicial independence, an effective Election Commission, an autonomous Anti-Corruption Commission, a National Ombudsman and a merit-based civil service are elements of what constitutional theory calls horizontal accountability: State institutions checking other state institutions.
John Rawls wrote that “justice is the first virtue of social institutions.” Institutional reform is therefore not an administrative luxury; it is the condition under which public power becomes legitimate.
In foreign affairs, “Bangladesh first” rests on strategic autonomy, reciprocal realism, and sovereign equality. Relations with India require cooperation on trade, borders and equitable water sharing without compromising national interests.
Chinese investment should satisfy transparency, debt-sustainability, and local employment tests. Ties with the United States and European Union remain essential for trade and technology, while partnerships with Turkey and the Islamic world can support energy, defense and action on the Rohingya crisis.
Several tensions nevertheless require vigilance.
Majority heritage must never dilute minority equality; national unity must not be used to silence opposition, journalists, academics, or peaceful protest. Support for domestic industry must not become protection for politically connected monopolies.
Constitutional amendments alone cannot change political conduct. Most importantly, the doctrine must be judged through measurable outcomes: Minority-security data, healthcare coverage, poverty reduction, youth employment, judicial independence, local-government capacity, corruption control, and electoral transparency.
Karl Popper’s idea of the open society is pertinent: Democratic strength lies in the capacity to correct policy through criticism rather than suppress criticism in the name of unity.
The movement from Bengali nationalism to Bangladeshi nationalism and then to “Bangladesh first” reflects changing stages of nation-building. Bengali nationalism generated liberation; Bangladeshi nationalism supplied a territorial civic identity; Tarique Rahman’s doctrine seeks to carry that tradition into institutional reform and developmental governance.
Its ultimate value will depend not on slogans but on the quality of citizenship it creates. A strong nation is one in which families possess social security, farmers receive fair prices, young people acquire useful skills, local communities share power, minorities worship without fear, Parliament restrains the executive, and diplomacy protects sovereignty without producing isolation.
Properly interpreted, “Bangladesh first” places neither the state above the citizen nor the majority above the minority. It places human dignity, constitutional equality, accountable institutions, and the collective welfare of the people above partisan advantage -- and thereby offers a possible ethics of democratic statecraft.
Prof Dr Saiful Islam is a political analyst and teaches at the University of Dhaka.

The newly signed memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Bangladesh and China to expand cooperation in technical education and skills development is an excellent step, and one that aligns directly with one of our country’s most urgent development needs.
Bangladesh’s economy in recent years has been held back not by a lack of ambition, but by a shortage of skilled workers. In addition, despite calls for technical education needing more investment and attention, those calls have often fallen on deaf ears.
To that end, that Bangladesh and China will now cooperate in vocational training programs, bilingual educational materials, vocational education research, industry-education integration, industrial training in Bangladesh, study visits to China, and specialized training programs for vocational education, can only be seen as a positive step.
This agreement has the potential to begin strengthening the very foundation of our workforce. As the economy evolves - with growing opportunities in ICT, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, and other relevant sectors - the demand for technically-trained workers will only continue to rise. Yet too many young Bangladeshis still enter the job market without the skills employers need.
Partnerships like this can help close that gap. China has extensive experience in technical and vocational education, and Bangladesh stands to benefit from knowledge transfer, modern equipment, and updated training standards.
If implemented effectively, this cooperation can produce graduates who are more competitive, more employable, and better prepared for both domestic and international job markets.
Bangladesh cannot rely on low‑skill labour indefinitely. To move up the value chain, investing in people, especially the youth, is the only logical step. This MoU is therefore a welcome move, but it must be followed by sustained commitment.
Strengthening technical education is essential for building the Bangladesh of tomorrow. This is what must be recognized.

The Makkah defense pact and Bangladesh: A test of strategic autonomy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
From the Middle East to South Asia, the strategic map is changing rapidly. Prolonged wars, regional conflicts, economic uncertainty, and intensifying rivalry among major powers are prompting states to rethink how they secure their national interests.
One of the most significant recent developments is the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, signed in Makkah on August 7, 2026 by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan. The agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all three, while also calling for broader defense cooperation.
For Bangladesh, the issue is no longer merely whether it should join the Makkah framework. The larger question is how Dhaka can develop a defense and foreign-policy strategy that maximizes its security options without becoming strategically dependent on any single power or drawn into conflicts unrelated to its national interests.
Recent statements from Bangladesh indicate that Dhaka is keeping the possibility of participation open. Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir has said that Bangladesh views the possibility positively but would consider any such arrangement in light of its national interests and the changing global environment. This is not the same as a decision to join, but it makes the strategic debate increasingly relevant.
More than an “Islamic NATO”
The Makkah agreement has understandably been described in some quarters as an emerging “Islamic NATO.” Such a description, however, is premature. NATO possesses a highly developed institutional structure, integrated command arrangements, and decades of operational experience. The Makkah framework is at a much earlier stage.
Nevertheless, its political and strategic significance should not be underestimated. Saudi Arabia contributes enormous financial resources and considerable geopolitical influence; Türkiye brings a sophisticated and increasingly autonomous defense industry, NATO experience and advanced capabilities in drones, electronic warfare, and other military technologies; while Pakistan contributes a large and experienced military and nuclear capability.
The agreement therefore brings together three complementary sources of strategic power. If implemented effectively, it could eventually facilitate greater cooperation in defense production, military training, intelligence, technology transfer, and collective deterrence. Türkiye's foreign minister has also indicated that the pact is not directed against any particular country and that other states could potentially participate in the future.
Why now?
The emergence of the Makkah framework must be understood against a rapidly deteriorating regional security environment. The Israeli strike on Hamas leadership in Doha in 2025 demonstrated that even states traditionally viewed as relatively secure could find themselves exposed to the spillover effects of regional conflicts. Qatar, an important mediator between Israel and Hamas, condemned the strike as a violation of its sovereignty.
The subsequent escalation of regional tensions, including the 2026 Iran-related conflict and attacks affecting Gulf security, has reinforced the perception among regional powers that they cannot rely indefinitely on external security guarantees.
The Makkah initiative can therefore be interpreted partly as an effort to strengthen regional strategic autonomy. It does not necessarily represent a rejection of the United States or existing alliances. Rather, it reflects a broader trend in which regional powers seek greater capacity to manage their own security environment.
What could Bangladesh gain?
Bangladesh has legitimate reasons to examine the development carefully. Its defense capabilities remain significantly dependent on imported equipment and technology. Türkiye's growing defense industry could provide opportunities in drones, unmanned systems, naval platforms, electronic warfare, and defense manufacturing. Saudi Arabia offers financial strength and investment potential, while Pakistan has extensive military experience and established institutions for military education and training.
Bangladesh already maintains separate relationships with all three countries. Saudi Arabia is important to Bangladesh because of labour migration, remittances, investment, energy, and broader political and cultural ties. Türkiye is becoming an increasingly important economic and defense partner. Relations with Pakistan remain historically sensitive because of the legacy of 1971, but contemporary diplomatic, economic, educational, and military contacts have expanded.
A carefully designed engagement with the Makkah framework could therefore offer Bangladesh three potential advantages:
But these benefits must be weighed against substantial risks.
Bangladesh's security environment is different
The principal weakness of simply joining an existing security framework is that Bangladesh's security priorities are not identical to those of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, or Pakistan.
Saudi Arabia's primary security concerns are centred on the Gulf and the wider Middle East. Pakistan's strategic calculations are deeply influenced by India, Afghanistan, and South Asian military competition. Türkiye's security environment encompasses Europe, the Black Sea, the Middle East, and its NATO commitments.
Bangladesh's priorities are different: Relations with India, the Bay of Bengal, the situation in Myanmar and Rakhine, border security, maritime trade routes, the Indian Ocean, and emerging climate-related security challenges.
Consequently, Bangladesh should not automatically adopt another country's threat perceptions as its own.
This distinction is particularly important because of the collective-defense provision. If Bangladesh were to become a formal member of a pact under which an attack on Pakistan could potentially trigger obligations toward Pakistan, India's assessment of Bangladesh's strategic orientation would inevitably change. Defense cooperation with Türkiye is one thing; participation in a collective-defense arrangement involving Pakistan is strategically much more consequential.
Managing India, China, and the United States
India would naturally watch any Bangladeshi move toward the Makkah framework closely. Bangladesh therefore needs to avoid creating the perception that its defense policy is being directed against India.
China would also have strong reasons to monitor developments. Pakistan is one of Beijing's closest strategic partners, while China maintains substantial economic and diplomatic relations with Türkiye and Saudi Arabia. Bangladesh itself is an important Chinese economic and defense partner. Greater Bangladeshi diversification of defense relationships could therefore encourage Beijing to strengthen rather than reduce its engagement with Dhaka.
Washington would view the development through the wider lens of the Indo-Pacific. Bangladesh's strategic location along the Bay of Bengal makes its foreign and defense policies relevant to maritime security and the wider Indo-Pacific balance.
This is where Bangladesh's diplomatic skill will be tested.
From weapons buyer to technology partner
The most important lesson for Bangladesh is that defense diplomacy should not be reduced to purchasing weapons.
Buying fighter aircraft from one country, drones from another, and missiles from a third may diversify suppliers, but it does not necessarily create strategic autonomy. Bangladesh could remain a permanent consumer in the global arms market.
A more ambitious objective would be to acquire technology, production capability, and knowledge.
Bangladesh should explore joint development and local production of drones and unmanned systems, military electronics, surveillance equipment, communications systems, and selected naval technologies. Cooperation with Türkiye could be particularly valuable in this regard. Defense-industrial cooperation can also stimulate research, skilled employment, technological innovation, and broader industrial development.
The strategic question should therefore change from “Where can Bangladesh buy weapons?” to “How can Bangladesh become a partner in developing and producing defense technology?”
A better option: Diversified defense diplomacy
For Bangladesh, the most realistic strategy may be diversified and issue-based defense cooperation rather than membership in a rigid military bloc.
Dhaka can deepen defense-technology cooperation with Türkiye; expand investment, training and maritime-security cooperation with Saudi Arabia; maintain selective military education, training, and peacekeeping cooperation with Pakistan; continue appropriate defense and technological cooperation with China; pursue maritime surveillance and advanced technological cooperation with the United States and European partners; and maintain pragmatic security cooperation with India on border management, maritime affairs, counterterrorism, and regional stability.
Such an approach would maximize Bangladesh's options while minimizing dependence.
Three principles should guide any future defense agreement.
First , Bangladesh should avoid joining a military alliance explicitly directed against another state.
Second , Bangladeshi territory should never become a foreign military base or a platform for military operations against another country.
Third , Bangladesh should avoid excessive dependence on any single country's weapons, technology or defense infrastructure.
A fourth principle is equally important: Before entering any major security agreement, Bangladesh must assess not only the immediate military benefits but also the economic costs, diplomatic consequences, and potential obligations that could arise during a future conflict.
Strategic autonomy, not strategic isolation
The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement could become an important new element in the security architecture of the Middle East and the wider Muslim world. Whether it remains a limited trilateral arrangement or evolves into a broader regional framework is still uncertain. What is clear, however, is that the agreement has opened a new strategic conversation.
Bangladesh should therefore watch the initiative closely rather than rush toward membership. If a formal proposal for participation emerges, Dhaka should evaluate its precise obligations, military benefits, economic costs, and diplomatic consequences before making a decision.
Bangladesh's national interest would not be served by entering an arrangement in which another country's war automatically becomes Bangladesh's war.
The country's strategic objective should instead be strategic autonomy without strategic isolation.
Bangladesh's greatest strategic asset is not a fighter aircraft, missile, or military alliance. It is geography. Situated at the intersection of South Asia and Southeast Asia and facing the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh occupies a position of exceptional strategic importance.
If that geographical advantage is combined with effective diplomacy, economic strength, technological capacity, and credible national defense, Bangladesh can become not a follower of another country's security architecture but an influential regional actor in its own right.
The goal, therefore, should not be to choose one camp over another. It should be to build a network of partnerships in which different countries cooperate with Bangladesh in different areas, while Bangladesh retains the freedom to determine when, where, and how its national interests require engagement.
Dr Nasir Uddin Ahmed is a retired Major, researcher and political/security analyst. Email: directtoradmin2007@gmail.com .

item.description:
The planned $550 million Laldia Terminal is one of the most ambitious port projects Bangladesh has taken on - one that has the potential to reshape Chittagong.
A modern terminal with expanded capacity, efficient cargo handling, and improved connectivity is exactly what we need to keep pace with rising export volumes and global shipping demands. Above all else, this is what we need as Bangladesh looks to take the meaningful next step in its development journey.
Done right, this could become a cornerstone of Bangladesh’s economic future, but ambition alone is not enough. We have seen too many large infrastructure projects suffer from delays, cost overruns, and coordination failures. The Laldia Terminal cannot afford to join that list.
Given that the port is projected to be made entirely with foreign investment, there is an even greater need to ensure this is done right. Foreign investment continues to be a challenge for our nation, and ensuring the port development stays on track is one way to instil confidence into future investors.
As such, this project must be executed with discipline: Strict adherence to timelines, transparent procurement, and rigorous oversight.
Moreover, future development for Bangladesh must be built upon the principles of sustainability, with a clear operational plan that ensures projects deliver the benefits promised.
If implemented properly, the terminal will strengthen Bangladesh’s position in global supply chains, support export‑led growth, and ease the strain on existing port facilities. It is a project that can genuinely transform Chittagong -- but only if it is treated with the urgency it deserves and not yet another slow‑moving development scheme.
Bangladesh needs this terminal. Now it must prove it can deliver it -- on time, on budget, and with the seriousness our future demands.

Saving the Sundarbans from criminality. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The reopening of the Sundarbans is welcome news for thousands of fishermen, forest workers, and others whose livelihoods depend on the forest. It is unfortunate to note, thus, that piracy has once again become a serious threat in the area.
While many finally have an opportunity to return to work after three months of closure, and begin recovering from the financial strain that has accumulated in their absence, returning to the forest also means returning to fear.
Fishermen have reported being forced to pay extortion money to criminal groups in exchange for so-called tokens or slips that supposedly allow them to enter particular parts of the forest safely. Those who refuse can face abduction, assault and ransom demands.
For some locals, the threat from pirates has become more frightening than the forest's natural dangers.
This is unacceptable; people should not have to choose between risking their lives and abandoning their livelihoods.
These communities already live with poverty, debt, and the uncertainties of climate and nature. The return of organized criminal groups should not add another burden to their lives.
There have been encouraging efforts: Recent Coast Guard operations have resulted in arrests, weapons seizures, and the rescue of hostages, while several groups and their members have surrendered.
But sporadic successes cannot substitute for sustained security. Authorities must intensify coordinated patrols, intelligence gathering, and surveillance throughout the forest and its waterways.
Law enforcement agencies must also establish reliable channels through which fishermen can report threats without fearing retaliation.
Most importantly, those who finance, organize, and participate in these criminal networks must face justice.
The Sundarbans belongs to the nation, but its protection is inseparable from protecting the people who depend on it. A forest cannot truly be considered secure when the communities entering it for their livelihoods remain unsafe.
Making the Sundarbans safe for all who depend on it must be treated as a priority.

item.title: Reassess the economics of the Bay Terminal. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is aspiring to become a trillion-dollar economy, an export powerhouse, and a future regional manufacturing hub. Given these ambitions, investing in world-class ports sounds like an obvious step.
But successful nations are rarely defined by how much infrastructure they build. Instead, they are defined by the discipline they bring to the decision making around what to build, when to build it, and at what cost.
That is precisely why the Bay Terminal deserves a fresh, evidence-based reassessment.
If Bangladesh can unlock substantially more capacity from the ports it already has, shouldn't we wring out those gains before committing billions more to another mega-project while our purchasing power is already strained?
That question is no longer theoretical. In 2025, Chittagong Port Authority handled a record 3.409 million TEUs of containers -- including roughly 750,000 empty boxes -- while carrying 92% of Bangladesh's international trade and nearly 98% of its containerized cargo.
For an economy this size, a port carrying that much of the national trade load is not merely infrastructure. It is the country's economic heartbeat.
Yet beneath the headlines about new megaprojects sits a less-told story. Operational assessments suggest that simply modernizing what already exists -- the New Mooring Container Terminal, the Chittagong Container Terminal, the general cargo berths, and a fully utilized Patenga Container Terminal -- could lift annual handling capacity from roughly 34 lakh TEUs to about 46 lakh TEUs according to a study.
That is a nearly 35% increase without building a single new deep-sea terminal -- on its own, roughly equivalent to adding the throughput of a mid-sized port.
The picture becomes more compelling still. Matarbari Deep Sea Port is already under construction, and the completion of its first phase is projected to lift Bangladesh's total container handling capacity to approximately 54 lakh TEUs -- almost a 60% increase over current throughput. Add APM Terminals' new facility and Matarbari's second phase, and overall national capacity could reach around 88 lakh TEUs -- roughly 2.6 times what the country handles today.
These numbers invite an obvious policy question: Should Bangladesh first optimize, modernize, and fully use the capacity it already has -- and the capacity already nearing completion -- before committing to another capital-intensive port expansion?
This is not an argument against development. It is an argument for sequencing it well.
Singapore continuously modernizes its existing terminals while sequencing expansion decades in advance. The Port of Rotterdam invests as heavily in automation, hinterland connectivity, and logistics integration as it does in physical infrastructure.
Busan's competitive edge comes as much from operational productivity as from additional berths. In global port economics, capacity is one variable, productivity is the multiplier.
That distinction matters because of opportunity costs. Bangladesh remains a capital-constrained economy, and every additional billion dollars committed to one project is a billion dollars unavailable for energy security, rail connectivity, inland logistics, climate resilience, education, or healthcare.
Infrastructure planning, in that sense, is an exercise in capital allocation as much as engineering.
This is where the Bay Terminal deserves closer scrutiny. Accommodating larger, deep-draft vessels will require substantial capital dredging, along with recurring maintenance dredging over the life of the project.
One estimate places initial dredging costs at$150-160 million, with annual maintenance potentially reaching $20-25m -- though these figures need independent engineering validation.
For scale, the World Bank has already approved a $650m loan to help finance the breakwater and access-channel dredging alone, a reminder that headline dredging estimates for the project tend to be a floor rather than a ceiling.
These costs are not, by themselves, reasons to abandon the project. They are reasons to make sure every assumption behind it is rigorously tested.
Bangladesh has already learned this lesson once, at Payra. That port's experience shows how sediment dynamics, navigation constraints, and long-term dredging needs can significantly affect operational economics over time.
Bay Terminal is a different project with different engineering characteristics, and the two should not be treated as identical. But Payra is a reminder that a port's success is measured not by its ribbon-cutting ceremony, but by its ability to operate efficiently, sustainably, and economically over the following 30 years.
Encouragingly, reports indicate that the Bay Terminal feasibility assessment is being revisited. That should be welcomed. It is an opportunity to do something Bangladesh has rarely attempted: A comprehensive national port optimization strategy.
Rather than evaluating Bay Terminal in isolation, policy-makers should weigh it against every realistic alternative such as modernizing NCT and CCT, fully utilising Patenga, accelerating Matarbari, improving rail and inland container logistics, expanding automation, and widening private-sector participation.
Only then can the country work out which sequence of investments delivers the highest economic return per taka spent.
The debate, then, is not whether Bangladesh needs the Bay Terminal. It is whether the Bay Terminal should be the next investment or whether smarter, faster, and more cost-effective options can deliver the same economic benefits while preserving scarce public resources.
Nations rarely grow prosperous because they build the biggest infrastructure. They grow prosperous because they build the right infrastructure, at the right time, in the right sequence, with the discipline to question even their most ambitious ideas.
As Bangladesh charts its maritime future, that discipline may prove to be the most valuable investment decision of all.
Ashfaq Zaman is the founder of Dhaka Forum and a strategic international affairs expert.

item.title: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries. [ dawn ]
item.description:
A two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel on Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis.

With more than 40 per cent of children under five stunted, a maternal mortality rate of 155 deaths per 100,000 live births, and malnutrition costing Pakistan upwards of $17 billion annually, the country stands at a crossroads: continue on the current trajectory and surrender an entire generation’s potential, or choose a different future.

The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action.

The focus of discussions will be on moving the national conversation beyond statistics towards practical, measurable interventions that can improve nutrition outcomes and protect Pakis­tan’s human capital and future generations.

View the full agenda here.

11:25am - Doctor says nutrition the ‘outcome of many systems’

Dr Aminah Jahangir, the global lead for health and nutrition at the Aga Khan Foundation, said that nutrition is the outcome of many systems and cannot be solved by one. She said that climate was already shaping the conditions in which children grow.

“Our experience suggests that the outcomes are better where health services, food systems and community institutions have worked around the same household over many years. It reminds us that progress is achievable in our own context,” she said.

11:12am: WFP official says over 80pc of stunted children come from middle-income countries

Asia Pacific Regional Nutrition Adviser for the World Food Programme Nora Hobbs, in her address, spoke of the geographical realities of stunting, stating that the majority of children affected by stunting are from middle-income countries.

“Over 80pc of the world’s stunted children are in middle-income countries,” she said.

The WFP official continued: “This means that low-income countries may have the highest rate and prevalence, but because middle-income countries have such a large population, it may have higher numbers of stunted children.”

She stressed that the facts highlighted that stunting was a result of “inequalities within countries”.

11:05am - Expert highlights need for coordinated response

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, said that neither food nor the health systems could solve malnutrition alone.

“Progress requires coordinated action across food systems, health systems and social protection. Countries that built integrated approaches before crisis struck, were able to keep essential services running through disruption,” he said.

“Integration cannot be improvised during a crisis. It has to be done in advance,” he said.

11:00am - Expert says 2.6bn people cannot afford a healthy diet

Dr Giacomo Zanello, an associate professor of Food Economics and Health at the University of Reading, presented a report on global nutrition.

“Around the world, progress on nutrition is under increasing pressure. Climate shocks, conflict, economic uncertainty … are affecting food and health systems,” he said.

He said that the 2026 global nutrition report focused on how countries can build healthy diets, through stronger integration of food and health systems while building resilience.

“Today, 2.6 billion cannot afford a healthy diet,” he said. He said that extreme weather, rising food prices and pressure on health services were arriving alongside conflict and instability, which was affecting food and health systems.

10:55am - Session on global and regional realities begins

The session on global and regional realities has now begun.

10:52am - UN official says nutrition should not be activated only after a crisis

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that communities must be at the heart of the response to malnutrition and stunting.

“Investing in front line workers and community-based platforms and listening to communities themselves can strengthen the uptake of essential services and practices, reinforce local ownership and ensure that women and children most at risk are reached,” she said.

She said that Pakistan knew better than most how quickly climate disasters, economic shocks and displacement can undermine years of development programmes.

“Nutrition, therefore, cannot be something we activate only after a crisis. It needs to be built into the preparedness, into the anticipatory action and the shock responsive systems so that vulnerable families are identified beforehand,” she said.

10:46am - UN official says malnutrition an ‘emergency we can no longer ignore’

Pernille Ironside, the United Nations’ resident coordinator in Pakistan, said that malnutrition was an “emergency we can no longer ignore”.

“When we talk about nutrition, we are not only talking about what a child eats. We are talking about whether a child reaches their full potential. We are talking about the strength of Pakistan’s capital. Nutrition is not only a health issue, it’s a development issue, an economic issue and an issue of equity and opportunity,” she said.

She said that children living in poorer and remote areas were more likely to be left behind. She also said that at the same time, Pakistan faced a growing burden of obesity-related diseases.

10:40am - World Bank official says malnutrition barrier to health, prosperity of individuals, nations

Abigail Perry, the lead nutrition specialist at the World Bank, said malnutrition was a fundamental barrier to the health and prosperity of individuals, communities and nations.

“When a child’s development suffers early in life, the effects can last a lifetime,” she said. She said that the challenge for Pakistan was how to act at the scale, speed and quality required.

10:35am - WHO chief says nutrition is not just about food

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said nutrition was not only about food.

“It is about access to safe, healthy, diets and strong food systems. Government, academia, civil society and the private sector all have a role to play,” he said.

10:30am - WHO chief says malnutrition one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity

World Health Organisation Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, in a recorded message, said that malnutrition remained one of the greatest barriers to health, development and opportunity.

“Every year, it contributes to millions of preventable deaths,” he said. He said that the problem was not a lack of knowledge, rather a lack of action.

10:20am - Minister says equity begins in the womb

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that the Pakistan of 2047 is being built today.

“It is being built in the health of our mothers. It is being built in the nutrition of our infants. It is being built in our homes and communities and it is being built in the developing minds and bodies of our youngest children,” he said.

“We all have to work as a whole,” he said, calling for the conference to spur action.

“Let this be our commitment: every child nourished is protected, every child given a fair start brings Pakistan one step closer to the future we seek,” he said.

10:10am - Minister says investment in nutrition is not charity

“Pakistan cannot win the economic race of the 21st century if millions of children begin the race of life several steps behind than others. There can be no knowledge economy without developing the capacity of the human brain. There can be no productivity revolution without healthy and capable workers. There can be no genuine equality if inequality begins before a child is even born,” said Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal.

“Therefore, investment in nutrition is not charity, it is economic policy,” he said.

10:03am - Minister says first 5 years of a child’s life critical

Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said that human resource development had not been prioritised in the past. He appreciated the initiative by DawnMedia Group to address the nutrition crisis and called on civil society to take up social issues.

“90 per cent of a children’s brain develops by the age of five .. so the first five years in the life of a child are the most critical,” he said.

“If we fail to develop that human infrastructure during the earliest years of life, we weaken every other investment we subsequently make,” he said.

“That is why stunting cannot remain merely a statistic. For the planning minister, it is a national development challenge,” he said.

9:57am - Planning minister says quality of human resource critical for countries

In his remarks, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, the chief guest, conveyed Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s firm commitment to addressing malnutrition and stunting as a national development priority.

He said that as the planning minister, he spent much of his time dealing with the architecture of Pakistan’s development.

“We discuss motorways, energy, dams and digital networks. All of these are essential, but there is one investment more fundamental than all others: the investment in human development,” he said.

“Ultimately it is humans and people who build nations. Therefore, the quality of human resource is critical for any country,” he said.

9:55am - Dawn CEO says nutrition crisis does not ‘look the same’ across the country

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said the nutrition crisis did not “look the same in Tharparkar as it does in Chitral or in southern Punjab”, adding that the response could not be the same either.

“You will hear the economics of financing nutrition, the science of why children fail to grow even when food is technically available, and, I hope, the voices of the women and the mothers who carry the heaviest share of this burden and are so rarely asked to speak about it,” she said.

“With all those who have a role to play gathered around the same table, we have an opportunity to move from recognition of the scale of the problem towards urgent, coordinated and measurable action — action that can improve maternal and child nutrition, strengthen Pakistan’s human capital, and give future generations the opportunity to grow, learn and thrive,” she said.

“That is what this conference ultimately aims to achieve: to build a shared understanding of what needs to be done, and to begin charting a clear and practical roadmap for how we get there,” she added.

9:53am - Dawn CEO says nutrition not a problem for health ministry to solve alone

Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that Pakistan loses close to $17 billion a year to the consequences of malnutrition, “more than what we typically borrow from the International Monetary Fund in any given year”.

“We spend enormous energy negotiating that borrowing. We spend comparatively little energy addressing a loss nearly as large, happening quietly, inside our own households,” she said.

“So this conference starts from a simple premise: nutrition is not a problem for a health ministry to solve alone. It sits at the intersection of health, agriculture, water, education, social protection, our economy and ultimately, our national security,” she added.

She said that countries such as Bangladesh, Peru, and Rwanda had demonstrated that stunting can be dramatically reduced within a generation, but “only when a nation decides, at the highest levels, that the future of its children is important enough to make it a collective priority”.

9:52am - Dawn CEO calls stunting crisis ‘a national emergency’

In her welcome remarks, Dawn CEO Nazafreen Saigol Lakhani said that four out of every ten children under the age of five in Pakistan were stunted.

“These are children whose physical growth and cognitive development may be permanently compromised – often before they have spoken their first words, entered a classroom or had the slightest chance to even dream of their own future,” she said.

“And when this is the reality for four out of every ten children in our country, we cannot merely call it a health problem. It is a national emergency – and a profound failure of our collective priorities,” she said.

9:45am - Conference begins

The conference has begun with the playing of the national anthem and the recitation of the Holy Quran.

item.title: Promises must be kept regarding the gas crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi has assured the public that normal gas supply will be restored by the first or second week of September. After what appears to be several weeks of severe shortages, factory disruptions, and household frustration, this is a commitment that demands scrutiny -- and follow‑through.
We are no strangers to repeated assurances about energy stabilization in the past, only to see the crisis persist. This time, the government must be held to its word.
While the crisis has rightfully been attributed to global instability, pointing to the US-Israel attack on Iran and the subsequent conflict and disruptions in shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, there is no denying that Bangladesh has not planned well when it comes to diversifying its energy sources.
Bangladesh’s domestic energy failures are a result of more than just global events, and the public deserves clarity, not deflection when it comes to them. The crisis has already caused widespread hardship, and citizens need solutions, not geopolitical narratives.
While Prime Minister Tarique Rahman allocating Tk40,000 crore to the energy and power sector to address the shortage is certainly a significant sum, it is meaningless if it does not translate into measurable improvements. Bangladesh has seen large allocations before, but without transparent implementation, spending alone does not guarantee relief.
The real test here is simple: Will households and industries actually experience the normalization promised by September?
Bangladesh cannot afford another cycle of promises without action. The gas and power crisis has undermined industrial output, strained household budgets, and weakened public confidence.
The government must deliver tangible results, and will be judged by whether gas actually flows again, not by statements made at press briefings.

item.title: Before the Earth moves. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The earthquake tragedy in Colombia last month should make Bangladesh ask a question that has little to do with predicting earthquakes: What happens when most of a nation's population, opportunity, and institutional capacity become concentrated in one city?
The United Nations projects Dhaka to become the world's largest city by 2050, with a population exceeding 50 million. Bangladesh already struggles with congestion, housing shortages, groundwater stress, pollution, inadequate sanitation, and enormous pressure on public services. Add tens of millions of people to this urban system, and earthquake vulnerability becomes only one dimension of a much larger human-development challenge.
Bangladesh already has projects designed to strengthen secondary cities, transportation corridors, and areas outside Dhaka. But the scale of the coming transformation requires something larger.
We should stop thinking primarily about moving people and start moving opportunities.
Start with those whose jobs may not survive
Walk through Dhaka and one sees an extraordinary amount of human effort.
A rickshaw puller pedals through extreme heat. A day labourer waits each morning hoping someone needs him. A young graduate rides a bicycle for deliveries because he cannot find work matching his education. A garment worker wonders whether automation will eventually replace part of her job. A rural worker leaves home because Dhaka appears to offer the only realistic path toward higher income.
These people are often described statistically as “labour.”
They are something much more important: Bangladesh's human capital.
The question is whether Bangladesh will continue using millions of people in occupations producing relatively little economic value and offering limited upward mobility or invest in enabling those same people to build the next economy.
Consider the rickshaw puller. The policy objective should not be to ban his rickshaw. That simply destroys income.
Ask instead: What could this person be doing 10 years from now?
Could he become a construction technician? A plumber? A logistics worker? A solar installer? A water-treatment operator? An emergency-response worker?
Then ask the more important question: What would it take to get him there?
That is human development.
Bangladesh may need housing and infrastructure for tens of millions of additional urban residents over the coming decades.
That sounds like a burden. It could also represent one of the largest employment opportunities in the country's history.
Building a network of 20 or 30 major economic centres would require enormous numbers of electricians, plumbers, welders, machine operators, construction workers, engineers, drivers, healthcare workers, water technicians, teachers, maintenance workers, and logistics professionals, among countless others.
Bangladesh already has much of the labour. The challenge is transforming skills.
Imagine a national program under which workers in vulnerable or low-productivity occupations receive paid training for three to 12 months. Training would be tied directly to employment.
The worker would not receive a certificate and then be told to search for a job. Infrastructure contracts receiving public support would commit to hiring qualified graduates.
The pathway becomes: Informal work → training → skilled employment → stable income → housing → financial inclusion → family security.
Urbanization then becomes a mechanism for social mobility.
Don't build another Dhaka
The objective should not be to create another megacity containing 30 million people.
Bangladesh needs a network.
Imagine economic centres distributed along existing and future rail, highway, and river corridors.
Some could specialize in healthcare and pharmaceuticals. Others in advanced textiles, food processing, logistics, electronics, renewable energy, technology, or light manufacturing.
Each would combine employment with housing, hospitals, schools, universities, parks, public transportation, and digital infrastructure.
That distinction is essential.
People do not move because planners draw circles on maps. They move because they can build better lives.
A family will leave Dhaka voluntarily when another city offers a good job, affordable home, safe school, reliable hospital, clean water, and reasonable transportation.
Bangladesh should therefore not attempt to redistribute population. It should redistribute reasons for people to choose where they live.
Water must come before homes
Water security should determine where these new centres grow.
Dhaka illustrates what happens when population growth outruns environmental infrastructure. The World Bank's current Metro Dhaka Water Security and Resilience Program describes serious pollution of rivers and canals resulting from rapid urbanization, inadequate sanitation, industrial discharge, and waste.
Bangladesh cannot sustainably replicate this pattern across the country. The next generation of cities should reverse the sequence.
Before approving hundreds of thousands of apartments, establish where their water will come from. Protect wetlands. Build reservoirs. Capture rainwater. Treat sewage. Recycle wastewater for industry. Protect groundwater recharge. Separate stormwater from sewage. Monitor industrial discharge digitally.
Bangladesh is one of the most water-rich landscapes on Earth, yet millions of citizens still experience problems involving safe drinking water.
That paradox demonstrates that water security is not merely about how much water a country possesses. It is about whether infrastructure delivers clean water to people when and where they need it.
Urban policy is health policy
The benefits would extend directly into national health.
A hospital treats disease after it occurs. A well-designed city can prevent some disease before the patient reaches the hospital.
Clean water reduces waterborne illness. Modern sanitation reduces exposure to pathogens. Cleaner transportation improves air quality. Better drainage reduces stagnant contaminated water. Trees and shaded streets reduce dangerous heat exposure. Walkable communities encourage physical activity. Shorter commutes give parents more time to their children. Formal employment makes health insurance and retirement savings more achievable. Distributed medical centres reduce the need for families across Bangladesh to travel to Dhaka for treatment.
For a country with limited healthcare resources, prevention through better living conditions may be among the highest-return health investments available.
Then there is the earthquake.
The magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia last month demonstrated again how quickly buildings, roads, and ordinary lives can be transformed by seismic disaster.
Bangladesh cannot know exactly when a major earthquake will strike the region. But Dhaka's vulnerability is well documented.
The answer cannot simply be more ambulances and rescue equipment.
If tens of millions of people, major hospitals, government institutions, financial organizations, and businesses remain concentrated within the same metropolitan region, Bangladesh is effectively concentrating national risk.
Developing multiple economic centres is therefore similar to diversifying an investment portfolio. If one region suffers catastrophe, the country continues functioning. Decentralization becomes national insurance.
Give Dhaka room to breathe
This strategy does not require abandoning Dhaka. It may be the best way to save it.
As future population growth increasingly occurs elsewhere, Dhaka can begin repairing the damage created by decades of uncontrolled expansion.
Unsafe buildings can gradually be replaced. Canals can be restored. Wetlands can be protected. Emergency roads can be widened. Schools and hospitals can be retrofitted. Waterways can again become environmental assets rather than drains.
Dhaka could become safer without becoming economically irrelevant.
The objective is not to weaken Dhaka. It is to make Bangladesh stronger than Dhaka alone.
Dr Mazher Mir is a Bangladeshi writer with over three decades of work on socio-economic and human development issues.

item.description:
The latest survey from Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA) on water pollution in Dhaka is nothing short of shocking: 424 outlets are dumping an estimated 330 tons of waste every single day into the Buriganga, Turag, Balu, and Shitalakkhya rivers around Dhaka.
To reduce this to mismanagement and oversight is no longer possible and must be called what it is -- environmental negligence on a staggering scale.
When a nation’s lifelines are treated as open sewers, the consequences are inevitable: Toxic water, collapsing ecosystems, public health crises, and a future that becomes harder to salvage with each passing year.
That out of the 424 identified discharge points, 244 are linked to privately owned factories and industrial establishments, tells us of the impunity enjoyed by industries in our country, where they have felt emboldened to continue polluting our rivers and affect millions of lives.
This feeble enforcement and non-existent accountability needs to be addressed with immediate effect.
Let it be reiterated: Dhaka’s rivers are dying because the authorities responsible for protecting them have failed to act. All the mandates, budgets, and legal powers mean nothing if there is no urgency to do what is right for the people of this country.
When 330 tons of waste enter the water system daily, “monitoring” and “future plans” are meaningless. Only decisive action matters.
The respected authorities must literally clean up their act. While the long term plan must include proper sewage treatment and enforcing effluent treatment requirements without exception, there is an immediate need to prosecute violators and ensure that sewer lines are not secretly connected to rivers.
Bangladesh cannot aspire to economic transformation while its rivers remain toxic drains. The numbers in this survey are a national embarrassment and must be treated as a call to action. The authorities must prove they are willing to act, not just talk.

item.title: Bangladesh hospital wards crowded as measles toll nears grim 1,000-child mark. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades is nearing the grim milestone of 1,000 child deaths, as a devastating epidemic sweeps through the country and crowded hospital wards fill with struggling babies.

Cries of sick children and the hiss of oxygen machines fill the air at Dhaka’s Shishu Hospital, where Rima Akter keeps a vigil beside her nine-month-old son.

“Just an hour ago, a child died, and they wheeled him out in front of us,” 30-year-old Akter told AFP on Thursday.

“We saw two children die today.”

Akter’s son Sabit Haque is one of scores filling the children’s hospital’s measles wards.

At least 986 children have died since March, while suspected and confirmed cases have surged past 180,000, according to the latest health ministry figures.

Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught.

Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems.

Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable.

The South Asian nation of 170 million has rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but case numbers continue to climb.

More than 1,000 suspected cases are reported daily.

‘Very weak’

“I’ve been running to and from multiple hospitals since July to get my son the proper treatment,” said Sanjana Islam Modina, 19, cradling her six-month-old son Ayan, who has an oxygen tube fixed to his nose.

Small dark spots covered Ayan’s head, fading from the angry red rash left by measles.

He was first admitted to hospital with pneumonia in July, then contracted measles before finally securing a bed at the capital’s specialised children’s hospital in mid-August.

Ayan spent 15 days in intensive care, before improving enough to return to the dedicated measles ward.

The hospital currently has 101 children admitted with suspected or confirmed measles.

“His lungs were already very weak from the pneumonia, then with measles his breathing was affected more,” Modina told AFP, while trying to soothe her wailing baby.

“He’s been on oxygen constantly for the last five days.”

Most cases recorded in Bangladesh during the current outbreak have been among children aged between six months and five years.

Doctors say many of the children arriving at hospital are already critically ill, with malnutrition further weakening their ability to fight the virus.

Ayan has also been diagnosed as malnourished.

“The doctors gave my son a special milk specifically designed for malnourished children,” said Modina, wiping sweat from his tiny forehead.

‘Devastating’

The outbreak has exposed gaps in Bangladesh’s efforts to protect its youngest.

SM Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for health, called the outbreak “devastating”.

Bangladesh had previously made major advances in vaccination against infectious diseases, but a measles drive planned for 2024 was delayed by the uprising that toppled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

Workers’ strikes and political instability delayed a 2025 campaign.

The country has since rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but the number of cases continues to climb.

“There was a gap of a significant number of children missing the doses,” Hyder said.

“Healthcare workers… are vaccinating these children to close the gap.”

Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), said Bangladesh should consider a broader vaccination campaign to contain the outbreak.

Rahman said public awareness was also crucial, stressing preventive measures including isolating infected children, handwashing and the use of masks by caregivers.

Worried mother Akter needs no reminder of how quickly the sickness can spread.

“We are aware of how contagious this disease is; our son was first admitted for bronchitis,” she said.

“After being released, we had to come back for measles.”

item.title: Things that lose money should close down. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Tea is an important part of life. I am an Englishman, and I would be betraying my entire culture if I didn't agree with that. But to say that being able to consume tea is important is not the same statement as trying to insist that certain tea plantations are important.
After all, as Adam Smith himself pointed out, “the sole purpose of all production is consumption.” As long as there is tea that we can brew up, the survival of a specific tea producer is of no matter.
Even the survival of an entire sector of tea production in one country doesn't matter. It's the being able to consume that matters, nor where produced nor who by.
This is the correct starting point for a consideration of this : “A revolving fund at a 6% interest rate to tackle the financing crisis in the tea sector.”
The inflation rate, at 8%, is higher than this 6%. The base rate at the central bank is near one and a half times that 6% at 9.5%. Commercial bank loans are at 12% and up.
So, the insistence here is that tea plantations should, effectively, be gifted free money.
Yes, obviously, the hope is that they'll pay it back, the money itself. But if they've not got to pay for the use of the money -- pay a real interest rate -- then that is the same statement as they get to use the money for free.
That's not a good idea.
The useful description of economics is that it's the study of the allocation of scarce resources. Resources are things like land, labor, and capital. We need to allocate them as best we can so as to make ourselves, collectively, as rich as we can. This means allocating those resources efficiently.
For there are always alternative uses of those resources. We could use the land of tea plantations for tea. We could put goats on it or solar panels. We could just go and stare at the awesome majesty of the mountains.
Whichever of those uses produces the greatest value to us consumers is the most efficient use of those mountain slopes.
We are gaining the greatest increase in the enjoyment of our lives by the use of those mountains to produce the greater value we can enjoy.
This is also obviously true of labor, of capital, and so on. We want to use our limited supplies of everything to produce the greatest amount that we can consume.
So, if the tea plantations cannot even pay us for the use of our money -- an interest rate below the inflation rate really is free money to a business, a loss to the rest of us -- then at least some of those tea plantations should no longer be in business.
They are not adding value, they are consuming more resources than they produce in value. They are a net loss to our society.
This is true of anything and everything in our society. Those things that are, nominally, businesses must produce more value than it costs to run them.
Otherwise they are all making us poorer -- the resources they consume are greater than the value of production, and yes, this really does mean they are making us all, in aggregate, poorer.
For we could devote those resources to things which add value, not subtract it.
If tea plantations can only survive by getting free money from the rest of us, then tea plantations should go bankrupt instead. Or at least some of them should, which will reduce the amount of tea produced. We'll all have to pay more for our tea, and that's the way the surviving ones will profit.
This is, of course, true of every other form of production in our economy. If it requires subsidy, then that's the grand clue that that form of production should not exist. Or, at least, less of it should.
I agree that it's a fairly harsh point to make, but things that lose money really should close down.
It's also fairly harsh to use tea plantations as the example, but, as at the top, I'm an Englishman. Tea is important; we really should get this right.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.
